every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Metoclopramide, which shares the same 4-amino-5-chloro-2-methoxybenzamide core as the query, is classified as having high adsorptive Caco-2 permeability (Papp >10 × 10^-6 cm/s), supporting adequate intestinal absorption for this scaffold.

Mosapride, a close benzamide analog, shows rapid and near-complete dissolution in acidic media (>95% at 10 min in 0.1 N HCl, Q5 97.49%, >90% in a hypoacidic stomach model) and 15 mg/ml solubility in PEG 400, supporting adequate dissolution for the benzamide scaffold.

Haloperidol has a measured F of 35 ± 8% (above the 20% threshold) despite high Caco-2 permeability (11.3–13.4 × 10^-6 cm/s), demonstrating that high permeability is consistent with F ≥ 20% and does not by itself imply low bioavailability.

L5 P-gp substrate records for sulpiride and amisulpride are mechanistically suggestive but involve different benzamide substituents (sulfamoyl/sulfonyl) and are low-transferability; they do not provide affirmative threshold-relevant evidence that the query is efflux-limited.

Flecainide and midodrine are described as well absorbed (BCS class 1, nearly complete, at least 90% absorbed), supporting that oral absorption is achievable for small-molecule drugs with moderate TPSA and low HBD; these are contextual, not direct query measurements.

Transfer from metoclopramide/mosapride is structural analogy, not direct endpoint evidence.
Potential P-gp efflux cannot be excluded for the query because some benzamide drugs are P-gp substrates, but no affirmative evidence supports it.
